briefOverview: Paul exhorts believers to live worthily by preserving unity and growing into mature Christlikeness through God-given gifts.
summary: Paul, writing as a prisoner, urges believers to walk worthily with humility, patience, and love, maintaining the Spirit’s unity in peace. He emphasizes the oneness of the church—one body, Spirit, Lord, faith, baptism, and God—and explains that Christ distributes gifts to equip leaders and members for building up the body toward mature unity and stability in truth and love. Christ, the head, coordinates the whole body so that every part contributes to growth in love. Believers must no longer live as the Gentiles do in futility and ignorance but must put off the old self and put on the new self created in righteousness and holiness. Concrete exhortations include truthfulness, self-controlled anger, productive work and generosity, edifying speech, not grieving the Holy Spirit, and replacing bitterness and malice with kindness, compassion, and forgiveness, as God forgave in Christ.
externalContext: Ephesians is widely regarded as a “prison epistle,” likely written while Paul was under Roman custody (commonly dated early 60s CE). Ephesus was a major Greco-Roman city known for commerce and the cult of Artemis; the church comprised many Gentile converts, which helps explain the contrast with former pagan ways. Early Christian communities organized around itinerant missionaries and local leaders; lists like apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors/teachers reflect emerging ministry roles oriented toward teaching and community formation. Moral exhortations using vice/virtue contrasts were common in Greco-Roman moral philosophy and Jewish wisdom traditions, here reshaped around Christ and the Spirit.
externalReferences: Verse 8 cites Psalm 68:18 (“When he ascended on high he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men”), applying a victory and procession psalm to Christ’s ascension and the distribution of spiritual gifts. “Be angry and do not sin” (v. 26) echoes Psalm 4:4. Paul’s body imagery and emphasis on diverse gifts serving one body parallels 1 Corinthians 12:12–27 and Romans 12:4–8. The “put off/put on” language and calls to truthful speech, love, and forgiveness closely parallel Colossians 3:9–14.

sectionTitles.title: Put Off Old, Put On New

practicalQuestions: How can I actively preserve unity in my community through humility, patience, and peacemaking?
Which gifts or responsibilities has Christ entrusted to me, and how am I using them to build others up?
What practices help me address anger quickly and righteously rather than letting it harden into sin?
Where do I need to replace unproductive or harmful habits with honest work and generosity?
Does my speech consistently build others up and impart grace?
Whom do I need to forgive, and what would it look like to forgive as God forgave me in Christ?
uncertainAreas: The meaning of “he descended into the lower parts of the earth” (vv. 9–10) is debated—incarnation, burial, or a descent to the dead are possible readings. Whether “pastors and teachers” (v. 11) denotes one combined role or two distinct offices is not explicit. “One baptism” (v. 5) may emphasize the shared rite of initiation and/or the Spirit’s work; the precise nuance is not specified in the text.
